importance 5/5 · 30 min · America’s $205 Billion Fund You’ve Never Heard Of | Conor Coleman · ▶ source

U.S. Development Finance Corporation — Strategy Pivot & Deal Flow Research Memo

Thesis

The DFC is undergoing a structural transformation from a concessional development lender into an active Wall Street-style strategic investor — deploying equity, mezzanine, and structured notes alongside legacy products — with $25B in authorized capacity over six years (~$4.2B/year). The mechanism for competing with China's BRI ($125B deployed last year alone) is a private-sector multiplier model requiring 3–4× capital co-investment per DFC dollar, making DFC a recurring anchor investor and deal-flow source for EM-focused alternative asset managers, sovereigns, and listed miners. Three near-term investable signals are already in the public domain: a named listed-equity holding (Syrah Resources, ASX: SYR), a named reinsurance counterparty (Chubb, CB), and a $1.8B (or $1.2B — see Confidence Zones) critical minerals vehicle with Abu Dhabi's ADQ.

Key Points

Mandate & Structure - DFC is the US government's international investment arm, reauthorized post-2025 with expanded toolkit: now includes common equity, structured equity, mezzanine, and structured notes in addition to prior senior secured loans, political risk insurance, and fund/bank intermediation. - Statutory investment cap is $25B over six years; 90% (~$22.5B) must be deployed in World Bank low-to-middle-income countries — a binding geographic constraint absent from most public commentary on DFC. This floors the vast majority of deployment in EM/frontier. - Seven priority sectors: (1) critical minerals, (2) transport/logistics infrastructure, (3) energy, (4) technology & telecom, (5) food security & agriculture, (6) healthcare, (7) financial services. Coleman identifies the first four as "bigger ticket items" under current administration priorities. - Target geographies: Latin America/Caribbean, Central Asia, Eastern Europe, Indo-Pacific; Africa currently 25% of Coleman's personal portfolio. - CEO: Ben Black (Senate-confirmed). Board: Commerce (Lutnick), Treasury (Bessent), State (Rubio). Not every transaction requires board sign-off; delegated authority exists at CEO level.

Belt-and-Road Gap - China deployed $125B through BRI last year — more than five times DFC's total authorized cap. Coleman acknowledges the gap; the multiplier thesis (2–4× private capital per DFC dollar) is the only credible path to volume parity. It is stated as aspiration; no historical mobilization ratio is cited.

Strait of Hormuz Reinsurance - Structured in under one month (DFC's fastest-ever deal) in partnership with Chubb as lead insurer; DFC provides ~50% reinsurance on hull & machinery, cargo, and P&I policies. - Not yet live. Open Questions for MacroDiscovery

  1. What is the actual statutory text of the DFC's 2025 reauthorization?   2. What is DFC's historical private capital mobilization ratio? Coleman asserts 2–4× co-investment per DFC dollar as the target, but cites no track record.   3. Who are the other named parties in the Orion CMC, and what is the confirmed total committed capital? "Orion and ADQ" — is Orion a mining company, a financial sponsor, or a US defense contractor? If three parties have each committed $600M, the vehicle is $1.8B in equity alone; the unconfirmed $500M debt layer would bring total to $2.3B. The structure, including whether DFC's offtake veto applies to ADQ's portion, has significant implications for how non-US allies participate.

  4. What is Syrah Resources' current US government equity ownership stake and at what valuation was the debt-for-equity conversion executed? If this is the first of several such transactions, the conversion methodology (discount to market? parity? structured premium?) sets a pricing template for future DFC public-market equity entries.   5. What specific operational threshold does the US military need to clear before activating the Hormuz insurance portal, and which command is responsible for that determination? Is there a defined coverage radius, escort ratio, or threat-level metric that triggers activation? The answer determines whether the Hormuz reinsurance is a weeks-away event or a condition that may not be met for months.

  6. Are there World Bank income classification edge cases that affect DFC's large-ticket priority geographies? Specifically: Kazakhstan, UAE, Saudi Arabia, and select Eastern European EU candidate states may be approaching or crossing upper-middle-income thresholds. If 90% of capital must go to non-wealthy countries, does reclassification of a major target country mid-authorization-period require portfolio reallocation, or is classification locked at deal inception? This matters for the longevity of any DFC-anchored investment thesis in fast-growing EM economies.

importance 5/5 · 68 min · Massive AI Crackdown Is Coming (It’s Simply Too Good) | David Woo · ▶ source

AI Capex Illusion, Frontier Model Regulation, and the Oil Trade — Research Memo

Monetary Matters / David Woo, Independent Economist

Thesis

The AI equity rally is built on three compounding illusions: nominal capex growth that is input-price inflation masquerading as volume demand, ARR growth partially inflated by mandated corporate consumption that is already unwinding, and an assumption of open frontier-model monetization that Woo argues is already being administratively throttled. The bear case is not that AI fails technically — Woo uses it two hours daily — but that its most capable iteration is too dangerous to distribute at scale, making the monetization curve priced into $5T of Nasdaq re-rating since April structurally inaccessible. Simultaneously, he holds a long oil position predicated on a game-theoretic read that Trump's public deal urgency has hardened Iranian resolve, making a near-term Hormuz resolution less likely than the market prices.

Key Points

Capex Accounting Mechanics - Combined capex of the five hyperscalers (MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, ORCL, META) fell quarter-over-quarter in Q1 — the first such decline in three years — and the year-on-year growth rate decelerated; real-terms contraction is larger still given component price inflation. - The earnings illusion: hyperscalers expense capex via depreciation (~10% in purchase period); component suppliers (Micron, SK Hynix) book 100% of price increases as revenue. A $100 price increase on the same chip creates $90 of aggregate EPS growth with zero incremental economic activity. This is the same accounting rules applied to an unusual degree, not a manipulation — but the scale exaggerates AI-sector earnings momentum materially. - Capex-to-operating-income for the five hyperscalers has reached 135%, forcing Google (seeking $80–85B equity raise) and Meta to issue external capital — a structural break from the era of self-funded investment. - Google and Amazon offset their Q1 capex pickup with a revaluation of Anthropic holdings — Woo's characterization: "totally artificial." - Microsoft and Meta pulled back Q1 capex; Microsoft lost its OpenAI exclusivity and corporate Copilot adoption has been "worse than expected." - Increased capex guidance from hyperscalers largely reflects paying more for the same volumes, not building more capacity — the homebuilder analogy: same 10 homes, $7M instead of $5M.

Demand Quality: Token-Maxing - Q1 AI consumption was inflated by corporate incentive structures (Amazon ranked engineers by AI usage), driving artificial demand — "token maxing." - Uber's COO stated publicly that the company burned its entire year's token budget in four months with little to show for it and is now pulling back. Woo relays this as a third-party data point, not firsthand knowledge. - Anthropic ARR grew from $9B to ~$42–44B, but Woo expects Q2 deceleration as token-maxing unwinds; Microsoft has also canceled most Claude licenses to push Copilot internally. - At least five LLM competitors now exist; the market is pricing "winner-take-all" dynamics in what is becoming a commoditized stack. Larry Ellison (per Woo citing Ellison) has said LLMs will commoditize because they train on the same public data.

Regulatory Risk: The Core Bear Case - Woo argues frontier model regulation is the dominant AI equity risk on a 6–12 month horizon — conditionally: "If Claude 3.5 turns out to be too dangerous, the regulatory blowback will be the biggest risk to AI on a 6-to-12-month basis." - Claude 3.5 Sonnet (referenced as "Mythos" by the host) is, per Woo's unverified claim, distributed to only ~150 users — two months post-release, "it's gone nowhere." He characterizes this as de facto government control already in effect. - Cyberattacks "went through the roof" starting last December; Germany cited €300B in cyberattack costs in a single year — the only non-US data point in the transcript. - A Trump executive order reduced the model release cooldown from a proposed 90-day period to 30 days; Woo views this as inadequate but acknowledges it is regulatory motion already underway. - Woo's regulatory logic is security/control, not populism: once a recursive self-improving model is distributed to 500–1,000 users, provenance becomes uncontrollable. If China acquires it, the response options are nil. - Trump's delay in a full crackdown is attributed by Woo to a desire to let Anthropic/OpenAI IPO "while the market is in a bubble" — a temporary brake on what Woo views as inevitable restriction. - AI will become "a huge political issue heading into the midterms."

Memory / HBM: Commodity Cycle, Not Secular Scarcity - HBM is structurally less complex than Nvidia logic chips; more competition exists and will increase. Chinese producers are advancing in DRAM and NAND flash; Woo states with high conviction they will reach HBM-level capability within 2–3 years. - Once new capacity comes online, prices drop quickly — the historical DRAM/NAND pattern. The "sold out into 2028" argument ignores the capacity cycle. - Short-term Q2 earnings deceleration is Woo's explicit near-term call.

Training→Inference Shift - AI workloads are migrating from training (GPU-intensive, Nvidia-dominated) to inference (less compute-intensive, more producers for NAND, CPUs). This deflates the compute-intensity and pricing-power assumptions embedded in current Nvidia multiples.

Oil / Iran - Woo is long oil, short equities, and short gold. - Hormuz throughput is "a very low number"; inventories are falling; unless a deal is reached, prices will "go through the roof." Trump's threshold is ~$150 before political pain forces action. - Game-theory problem: Trump's public urgency on a deal signals desperation to Iran, hardening their terms. Iran recently fired missiles at Israel — unprecedented — indicating they believe Trump is weak and are trying to drive a US-Israel wedge. Woo assesses near-term deal probability as low. - Most scenarios (no deal, escalation, partial deal with conditions) converge on higher oil prices; Woo does not need to call the exact outcome.

AI Productivity & Existential Tail - Woo believes AI is genuinely productive and uses it two hours daily; it can outperform the bottom 90% of workers on defined tasks. - It cannot replace the top 10% because it is "distilled consensus" — no original solutions, only recombination of prior work. 15 years of autonomous vehicle development with limited results is offered as a precedent for hype-reality gaps. - Critical hedge, missing from prior artifacts: "There is a scenario where AI brings about human extinction. These models are less predictable than previous ones. I don't know which endgame we're heading toward." Woo does not dismiss this tail; he expresses genuine uncertainty about the long-run outcome.

Best Quotes

1. The Earnings Illusion Mechanism

"Microsoft expenses $10, and Micron books $100. Combined earnings go up by $90 just because Microsoft is paying $100 more for the same chip. Ironically, the inflation of the components that go into data centers has given a boost to nominal earnings growth because equity investors look at nominal rather than real." — David Woo

Significance: Precise accounting mechanism explaining why AI-sector EPS acceleration is a price artifact, not a volume signal. Directly indicts the "beat-and-raise" cycle as partly illusory.

2. De Facto Regulation, Already In Place

"Claude 3.5 Sonnet has only been given to 150 users. Two months later, it's gone nowhere. That is de facto government control." — David Woo

Significance: Argues that the monetization ceiling on frontier models is not a future regulatory risk but a present operational reality — making the $5T Nasdaq re-rating premised on open deployment structurally impaired. (Note: the 150-user figure is Woo's unverified assertion; no source cited.)

3. Control, Not Popularity

"It's not about popularity; it's about control. If you give access to 500 or 1,000 people, you can no longer be sure who has it. If there is a major hacking event, you lost control. These models have recursive learning capability — they can create the next version without human intervention." — David Woo

Significance: Reframes the regulation thesis from political risk to national security imperative — a more durable and less reversible policy logic than legislative cycles or approval ratings.

4. The Funding Cycle's Circular Logic

"If you go into a recession, advertising — which is 85% of Google and Facebook's revenue — will drop. Everybody is giving money to Anthropic and OpenAI to keep them afloat to keep this cycle going. Nvidia is happy to invest in them to maintain that momentum." — David Woo

Significance: Exposes circular capital flows sustaining the AI ecosystem. In a macro downturn, the advertising revenue base and the strategic investment subsidy unwind simultaneously — a double-hit the "AI is recession-proof" consensus misses.

Disagreements & Conviction

Capex Growth Is Real [CONSENSUS] vs. It's Input Inflation [WOO — High Conviction] Woo offers specific mechanics: depreciation accounting, Google/Amazon's Anthropic revaluation as an artificial offset to Q1 capex, and the capex-to-operating-income ratio hitting 135%. He states this flatly as an empirical claim. Conviction: high. No hedging language.

HBM Is Sold Out Into 2028 [CONSENSUS] vs. It's a Commodity Cycle [WOO — High Conviction, Moderate Timing] Woo explicitly acknowledges the bull argument and dismisses it as a peak-cycle sentiment indicator. Uses "I guarantee" on Chinese supply competition within 2–3 years — strong language but a wide window. Genuine contrarian vs. sell-side consensus; not consensus dressed as contrarian.

Regulatory Risk Is Future / Speculative [CONSENSUS] vs. It's Already Operating [WOO — Very High Conviction, Conditional] Woo's highest-conviction call. He describes the 150-user distribution cap as existing de facto control, the Trump EO cooldown reduction (90→30 days) as regulatory motion already in progress, and states with no hedging that more people will "talk like me in the coming months because it's inevitable." Key conditional: "if Claude 3.5 turns out to be too dangerous." The host concedes political plausibility but pushes back on Trump's willingness to act; Woo reframes to control logic, not popularity — a distinct and more durable argument.

Anthropic ARR Is Durable Growth [CONSENSUS] vs. Token-Maxing Distortion [WOO — Moderate-High Conviction] Woo does not quantify what fraction of the $9B→$42–44B ARR growth is noise. The Uber data point is one named example, not a systematic audit. He expects Q2 deceleration and cites Microsoft's license cancellation as early commoditization evidence. Conviction: moderate-to-high on direction, lower on magnitude.

AI Productivity Belief vs. Bearish AI Equity Stance [INTERNAL TENSION — Not a Contradiction] Woo uses AI two hours daily and believes it is genuinely productive. His shorts are on valuation and access, not technology failure. The PM should not read his Nasdaq short as a bet that AI doesn't work — only that it won't monetize at current multiples under regulatory and competitive pressure. The distinction matters for catalyst identification and position sizing.

Capex Bubble Denial vs. Dotcom-Bust Analog [INTERNAL SEMANTIC TENSION] Woo says "I wouldn't call it a bubble" then immediately says he "absolutely" sees a capex-level decline analogous to the dotcom bust and uses the phrase "while the market is in a bubble" when describing Trump's IPO incentive. Whether this reflects analytical care or public positioning caution, the PM should weight the descriptive content (forced equity issuance, token-maxing demand, regulatory constraint) over the label Woo applies.

1. Memory / HBM Supply Chain — Short Setup, 1–2 Quarter Catalyst The nominal earnings acceleration in Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung's semi division is price-driven, not volume-driven. When Q2 token-maxing unwind becomes visible in hyperscaler consumption data, the earnings illusion reverses for both buyer and seller simultaneously. Chinese memory producers are approaching competitive parity (Woo's 2–3 year claim, unverified but consistent with public CXMT/YMTC reporting elsewhere). Multiples are set against peak-cycle artificially elevated earnings. Affected: MU, SK Hynix (000660 KS), Samsung semi division, SOXX/SMH. Time horizon: Q2 earnings (1–2 quarters) for catalyst; 2–3 years for full cycle repricing.

Woo's claim (unverified) that Claude 3.5 Sonnet has reached only 150 users — and that this is already functioning as de facto government control — would mean the monetization optionality driving valuation is already administratively capped. Time horizon: Q2 results, July–August 2025.

4. Oil Long / Macro Reflexivity Risk — 3–6 Months Hormuz throughput is materially impaired (Woo: "a very low number"); inventories are falling; near-term deal probability is lower than market prices because Trump's public urgency signals desperation to Iran, hardening terms. Secondary: if oil reaches ~$150, it re-ignites inflation, constrains Fed optionality, and compresses tech multiples through the risk-free rate channel — a reflexive loop reinforcing the AI fundamental bear case simultaneously. Affected: XLE, XOM, COP, USO (long); Nasdaq (short via rate channel); TLT (short on oil-driven inflation); gold (Woo is explicitly short). Time horizon: 3–6 months on deal/inventory dynamics.

6. Anthropic IPO — Caveat Emptor Woo explicitly characterizes the "Mythos" (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) release as an IPO setup: "Anthropic going toward an IPO; they want everybody to oversubscribe." ARR numbers inflated by token-maxing, license cancellations by Microsoft, commoditization from five competitors, and the 150-user distribution cap (Woo's claim, unverified) collectively question the revenue quality and growth durability that an IPO would be priced on. Affected: Anthropic private-market valuation, crossover funds holding Anthropic paper. Time horizon: Pre-IPO positioning window.

importance 5/5 · 42 min · The Rise of the Full-Stack Builder and Hyper-Leveraged Generalist with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella · ▶ source

Microsoft Build 2026 — Satya Nadella on Frontier Intelligence, Harness Economics, and the Permission to Grow — Research Memo

Thesis

Microsoft's strategic bet is that every enterprise needs its own "frontier intelligence" — a private eval harness plus model-agnostic orchestration — rather than model ownership, and that this platform layer captures stickier economics than any individual model provider. The corollary is that benchmark-driven model competition commoditizes frontier labs faster than the market assumes, while the harness/eval layer and underlying SaaS data assets retain durable value. The social license to execute this buildout has a self-imposed 12–18 month tangibility deadline, after which permitting, regulatory, and public-opinion friction become binding constraints.

Key Points

Model & Platform Strategy - Microsoft's MAI model family is differentiated not by benchmark performance but by clean pre-training lineage plus a hill-climbing scaffold for building private specialist models. Nadella explicitly states public benchmarks "can be maxed" — private evaluation sets are the true IP moat. - The platform thesis: a platform is defined by creating more value outside it than it captures inside. Microsoft's job is to enable every company to "operate at the frontier with their own frontier intelligence." - Microsoft's harness (GitHub/Foundry) is explicitly model-agnostic — Llama, MAI, or any third-party model can plug in. This is a structural bet that model commoditization accelerates and platform stickiness migrates to the harness/eval layer.

Agentic Deployment Reality - Coding agents are already productive enough to break the IDE. Nadella runs 100-agent sessions and states chat-only artifacts are unworkable: "We now have to rebuild the IDE." Canvas UI is a near-term forced transition. - Agent-captured "traces" of human-AI collaboration are the new enterprise IP: "Training a 'company veteran agent' that learns through those traces is incredibly valuable. It should essentially go on the balance sheet." This is a new asset-classification framework, not a metaphor. - Nadella himself is building long-running Foundry agents for chief-of-staff workflow monitoring — signals genuine internal adoption, not just positioning.

Pricing & SaaS Economics - Per-user pricing is "an artifact of someone needing budget certainty." Consumption will be the next dominant model. - Outcome-based pricing structurally stalls: "People love outcome-based pricing until they actually have an outcome, and then it feels like giving away royalty." - Named admission: GitHub Copilot was mispriced as a per-seat product before the intensity of agent usage was understood. The repricing has already been executed. - The build-vs-buy equilibrium for AI-generated software will take "one full budget cycle" to resolve. Maintenance is the check on DIY euphoria: "AI can find security bugs, but someone has to fix them, and that burns tokens."

SaaS Data Assets - The underlying data model and business logic of SaaS applications "are still robust and valuable." The disruption is in packaging, not annihilation. Microsoft 365 as an exposed database (Work IQ) is the concrete illustration: accessing design meeting notes via a GitHub repo query is "10x the value" but requires rearchitecting how requests are served. - Enterprises with "inflexible" software vendors face displacement; flexible incumbents with exposed data models earn a reprieve.

Organizational Design - The Azure networking team's reconceptualization is Nadella's clearest organizational prescription: "Our job is not to do networking; it's to build the agentic system that does networking." They reframed their work as meta-work — building systems that do the work, not doing the work. He calls this "the lesson for any organization." - LinkedIn created a new "full-stack builder" discipline combining design, product, and engineering. Infrastructure roles (e.g., building RL environments for Excel) are becoming critical hard-engineering problems.

Social License & Infrastructure - The host's intro monologue states Azure built more capacity in the last 15 months than in its first 15 years. (Attribution: host's framing — Nadella does not restate or confirm this figure in his own remarks.) - Nadella's societal deadline: "We have 12 to 18 months to make this tangible… whether it's health outcomes or the ability to run a local store more efficiently, people need to see it for themselves." This is a credibility cliff, not a hopeful observation. - Community-level permission framing (separate statement, same interview): "Unless we are principled about ensuring the benefits are felt at the community level, we won't have permission to grow. It has to be real: energy prices, water replenishment, training, jobs, and the tax base."

Best Quotes

Quote 1 — Satya Nadella

"We know all the public evaluations out there can be maxed, so each company will have its own private evaluation. Every company having private evaluations might be the biggest intellectual property. If you have a private eval and you can switch from Model A to Model B and climb up, you're in control."

Significance: Non-consensus indictment of public benchmarks as competitive signals. The durable moat is the eval harness, not the model — directly challenges the bull case for closed frontier labs.

Quote 2 — Satya Nadella

"People love outcome-based pricing until they actually have an outcome, and then it feels like giving away royalty. So that debate will continue. There is no one model to rule them all."

Significance: Grounds consensus enthusiasm for outcome-based pricing with a behavioral observation from lived deployment experience. The GitHub Copilot reprice admission ("it was constructed as a per-user product before we understood the intensity of agent usage") makes this a closed empirical loop, not a musing.

Quote 3 — Satya Nadella

"Training a 'company veteran agent' that learns through those traces is incredibly valuable. It should essentially go on the balance sheet. We couldn't put human capital on the balance sheet before, but we can with these agents that hold tacit knowledge."

Significance: Introduces a new asset-classification framework. If enterprises begin treating trained agents as balance-sheet assets, it has implications for enterprise software valuation multiples, M&A logic, and audit exposure.

Quote 4 — Satya Nadella

"The data model and the business logic underneath a SaaS application are still robust and valuable. The challenge of the SaaS business model is that we packaged it one way, and now we have to learn how to unbundle and rebundle in new ways."

Significance: Direct pushback on the "end of software" thesis from the CEO of the largest enterprise software stack. Validates the unbundling disruption while defending the underlying data asset — the sorting question he leaves open is whether rebundling outpaces monetization destruction.

Disagreements & Conviction

1. Outcome-based pricing as the future vs. as a behavioral trap - Consensus: Outcome-based pricing is the natural, customer-aligned evolution for agentic AI. - Nadella (contrarian): Customers resist at the moment of value delivery because it "feels like giving away royalty." No single pricing model will dominate. - Conviction: Strong and grounded in the GitHub Copilot reprice — this is a settled view from a named mispricing event, not speculation.

2. "End of software" vs. SaaS data/logic retains durable value - Market framing: AI makes workflows cheap to generate, threatening incumbents existentially. - Nadella: The data model and business logic are "robust and valuable." The disruption is in packaging and rebundling, not destruction. Maintenance token-burn provides a natural floor for third-party software spend. - Conviction: Moderate. He defends the asset class while accepting the packaging disruption. [Inference: his incentive is to soften the bear case given Microsoft's own SaaS exposure — this should be discounted accordingly.]

3. Platform openness vs. first-party product competition (internal tension) - Platform thesis: "Having an open harness and letting all models come in is the skill." Microsoft's job is enabling every company to operate at the frontier. - Product reality: Microsoft simultaneously launched MAI models and competes directly in code, productivity, and security — categories where ISVs build on Azure. - Nadella's offered mechanism: "Network effects around intelligence are different because they learn from data — not necessarily 'lots' of data, but the few samples needed to understand what is novel." He argues that private data creates differentiated intelligence at every node, not just at the platform. This is a substantive (if incomplete) mechanism claim — not purely rhetorical. - Conviction: The mechanism is stated but unverified structurally. Historical precedent (Windows) is invoked without explaining why it will hold in a market where Microsoft is competing more directly with its ecosystem partners than it did during the PC era. The tension is real and unresolved.

4. Public benchmarks as competitive signal vs. as gaming-prone noise - Consensus: Benchmark leaderboards are the primary model-quality ranking. - Nadella: Public benchmarks "can be maxed." Private eval is the real IP. He volunteers this without prompting and elevates it to IP status. - Conviction: Strong. This is a direct indictment of the market's primary model-ranking tool.

5. AI triumphalism vs. 12–18 month tangibility deadline (internal tension) - Nadella announced sweeping capabilities at Build while simultaneously setting a self-imposed 12–18 month window to demonstrate societal benefit: "People need to see it for themselves." - This implicit concession — that broad societal benefits are not yet tangible — sits in tension with the morning's confident product announcements. - Conviction: The deadline language is the strongest time-bounded claim in the transcript. It frames a credibility cliff, not a goal.

Investment Implications

Implication 1 — Private Eval Layer Commoditizes Frontier Models (Non-consensus: market prices frontier labs as having durable enterprise pricing power)

If enterprise switching costs between models are determined by eval infrastructure quality — not model lock-in — frontier model providers lose pricing power faster than current valuations assume. The moat migrates to whoever owns the harness/eval layer. Model-agnostic platforms (Azure Foundry, GitHub harness) benefit from model commoditization because their platform value rises as switching becomes routine.

Second-order: The consensus trade — long frontier AI lab exposure — has a structural ceiling the market underweights. Firms building private eval infrastructure (synthetic eval generation, RLHF tooling, harness orchestration) become strategically critical.

Affected: Negative for single-model API pure-plays (OpenAI, Anthropic — both private); positive for $MSFT (Foundry/GitHub harness), $GOOGL (Vertex model-agnostic layer), $AMZN (Bedrock); Scale AI and Weights & Biases (private). Confidence: Medium — eval-as-IP is TRANSCRIPT-SUPPORTED; magnitude of pricing erosion is MODEL INFERENCE. Time horizon: 2–4 years.

Implication 2 — SaaS Per-Seat Pricing Is Structurally Broken; Multiple Compression During Repricing Transition (Non-consensus: consensus treats repricing as a one-time event, not a model-level disruption)

Agent sessions either massively expand consumption (revenue upside with cost spike) or displace human seats (revenue hole). Most current pricing models cannot predict which occurs at contract time. The predictability premium in SaaS multiples — historically justifying 8–15x ARR — erodes as revenue becomes consumption-volatile, even if total revenue grows.

Second-order: Vendors who have already repriced to consumption get a volume upside surprise; those still on per-seat contracts face guidance volatility. The reflex short-SaaS trade is crowded; the non-consensus play is identifying names that have already transitioned (and are undervalued on legacy per-seat comps).

Timing signal: "One full budget cycle" (Nadella's framing) before enterprise equilibrium emerges — approximately 12–18 months from now.

Affected: $CRM, $NOW, $WDAY, $HUBS, $ZM; $MSFT (already in transition per the named GitHub Copilot example). Confidence: High — TRANSCRIPT-SUPPORTED with a named example; timing of cycle is MODEL INFERENCE. Time horizon: 1–3 years.

Implication 3 — Maintenance Costs Check the "End of Enterprise Software" Bear Thesis (Non-consensus: bears assume cheap code generation eliminates incumbent data moats)

The bear case requires zero-maintenance AI-generated code. Nadella explicitly pushes back: security patching, token burn for debugging, and governance overhead make full DIY uneconomic. "The next phase is: 'What software do I really want to generate versus use from others?'" Enterprise software incumbents with deep vertical workflow data are more durable than the bear case implies — conditional on flexibility. "Little tolerance for vendors who are inflexible" is the qualifier. The investable sort is between flexible and inflexible incumbents, not incumbents vs. DIY.

Affected: $SAP, $NOW, $WDAY, $ORCL (flexible, API-exposed names get reprieve); inflexible packaging-dependent incumbents remain at risk. Confidence: Medium — pushback on DIY is TRANSCRIPT-SUPPORTED; which specific incumbents survive is company-specific MODEL INFERENCE. Time horizon: 1–2 years (within one enterprise budget cycle).

Implication 4 — Social License Is an Underpriced Constraint on Data Center Capex (Non-consensus: infrastructure bulls treat capex as purely supply/demand for power and silicon)

Two distinct but related signals from the transcript — presented separately per QA audit:

Signal A (community permission): "Unless we are principled about ensuring the benefits are felt at the community level, we won't have permission to grow. It has to be real: energy prices, water replenishment, training, jobs, and the tax base." Nadella treats permitting and community acceptance as active management constraints, not background conditions.

Signal B (societal tangibility deadline): "We have 12 to 18 months to make this tangible… whether it's health outcomes or the ability to run a local store more efficiently." This deadline is framed as broad societal inclusion, not directly linked to data center permitting in the transcript. (The connection between Signal B and data center permitting risk is MODEL INFERENCE.)

If benefits remain concentrated and invisible to host communities, permitting friction, utility rate negotiations, and water/energy access could become binding capacity constraints. This is a tail risk to data center and power infrastructure earnings not in consensus models. Conversely, demonstrated benefits validate the bull case for power infrastructure with a longer runway than skeptics assume.

Affected: $EQIX, $DLR, $IRM; $VST, $CEG, $NRG, $AES; $VRT, $ETN, $HUBB; $NVDA, $AVGO (demand-side cap). Confidence: Medium on the social-license framing — TRANSCRIPT-SUPPORTED; Low on permitting-as-binding-constraint scenario — MODEL INFERENCE. Time horizon: 12–24 months.

Implication 5 — Microsoft's Model-Agnostic Harness Strategy Reduces Single-Model Dependency; Re-rating Catalyst If Execution Succeeds (Non-consensus: market treats MSFT AI as a proxy for any single model provider's success)

Nadella explicitly positions the GitHub/Foundry harness as model-agnostic ("you can use your Llama harness or any harness") and describes MAI as an internally built model lineage. The strategic framing is that Microsoft benefits from model competition rather than being tied to any single model provider.

[MODEL INFERENCE: Extrapolating this to a "structural decoupling" from any specific model partner goes beyond what Nadella states in this transcript. No model providers are named; the framing is model-agnosticism as a platform principle, not a statement about any specific relationship.]

If Microsoft successfully positions as the platform layer that benefits from model commoditization (see Implication 1), its AI business becomes structurally more valuable than a single-model proxy. A successful execution would re-rate $MSFT from "infrastructure + model reseller" toward "Windows of agentic AI." The risk: if proprietary MAI models underperform and the harness layer is not mature, the platform thesis fails to close before competitive pressure from $GOOGL and $AMZN intensifies.

Affected: $MSFT (positive re-rate on execution); $GOOGL, $AMZN (competing for the harness layer). Confidence: Medium — strategic model-agnostic intent is TRANSCRIPT-SUPPORTED; execution success and re-rating magnitude are MODEL INFERENCE. Time horizon: 2–3 years.

importance 5/5 · 34 min · Carmen Li's Plan to Build a Futures Market for Compute | Odd Lots · ▶ source

GPU Compute Futures — Research Memo

(Odd Lots, Carmen Lee / Silicon Data & Compute Exchange)

Thesis

GPU compute is in transition from a procurement cost to a hedgeable commodity, with CME-listed financially settled futures set to launch within months. The near-term data contradicts two dominant consensus trades: inference costs are not falling to zero (token prices doubled in ~6 months), and GPU assets are not depreciating rapidly (H100 residual values near par as of last year). The instrument designed to enable hedging carries structural limitations — definitionally ambiguous volatility metrics, basis risk, and a significant index-provider/spot-marketplace conflict of interest — that a PM must price before treating CME GPU futures as a clean hedge.

Key Points

Market Structure - Carmen Lee is founder/CEO of both Silicon Data (the GPU price index provider; CME settles against this index) and Compute Exchange (a competing GPU spot marketplace) — a dual-hat structure with no firewall or governance controls discussed in the transcript. This conflict is cross-cutting and affects every claim about index integrity below. - GPU futures and options on CME are launching "in a couple of months" pending CFTC approval; financially settled, accessible through standard futures brokers with conventional margin. - OTC forward contracts can be "physically delivered" — but delivery consists of API access to specific configurations, not a wafer. This introduces counterparty credit and SLA performance risk that does not exist in commodity physical delivery.

Index Methodology - Silicon Data ingests 150,000+ traded prices daily; total pricing database spans 8 million points from ~200 data sources. The daily ingestion draws from 100+ sources. - Normalization covers CPU, RAM, disk, geolocation, and memory bandwidth. Output is "highly correlated" but not equal to cloud provider prices — basis risk is structural and explicitly acknowledged. - Competing indices show divergent levels and trends. Lee's response: "the market always votes." Index methodology opacity is an unresolved risk; if the CME contract settles to Silicon Data's index and that index diverges materially from actual cloud costs, the futures fail their hedging function.

Volatility & Fungibility - Lee cites "20–30% daily volatility" for A100s and H100s. Critical caveat (QA correction): the term "daily volatility" is Lee's phrasing; the transcript does not clarify whether this is daily price-return standard deviation, intraday cross-sectional dispersion, or annualized vol. A true 20–30% daily return vol would annualize to ~315–475% — extreme by any commodity standard and inconsistent with "healthy." The actual metric is ambiguous and should not be used to size hedges without clarification. - Published research (with Jefferson Lab, presented at a GPO conference) shows 38% performance variance for the same GPU chip across providers — the primary fungibility challenge and the strongest evidence for structural basis risk.

Spot Price Signals - A100 rental prices up 10–15% in the past three months; B200 prices initially declined post-launch and have since recovered above launch price — both indicating demand/supply is tightening, not loosening. - Price per million tokens (blended input/output, consumption-weighted across 300 models tracked) has doubled since December 1, 2025 to approximately $2.21 — directly contradicting the consensus inference-deflation narrative.

GPU Asset Economics - As of last year per Lee's data: second-year H100 residual value ~85 cents on the dollar; third-year ~84 cents. Lee explicitly contrasts this with car depreciation. Temporal caveat (QA correction): this is lagged data from the prior period; given rapid generational GPU turnover, the figure may not reflect current marks. Lee also has a commercial interest in high residual values (she operates a refurbished chip business). - Data center build announcements do not translate to immediate GPU availability; servers, colocation, and fiber are sequential dependencies. This is a specific, unstated pushback on the headline hyperscaler capex narrative.

Institutional Participation - Some banks can cross positions internally; Lee wants dedicated compute trading desks but acknowledges GPU trading requires hardware, software, and regional supply/demand expertise — slowing desk formation. - Speculators are needed to provide liquidity, but financial settlement means early open interest will be dominated by directional bets, not hedgers — a standard early-stage commodity pattern.

Best Quotes

1. On basis risk and index utility

"This price will be highly correlated to the price you pay at a cloud provider. However, it won't be the same, just like basis trading in other commodities. There's a basis risk." — Carmen Lee Significance: The product's primary limitation, stated by its creator. Basis risk is structural, not solvable — PM must model this slippage before using CME futures as a procurement hedge.

2. On fungibility and the 38% variance

"We proved there's a 38% performance variance for the same chip." — Carmen Lee Significance: The single most important structural risk to index integrity. An index averaging across a 38% performance spread produces a settlement price that may bear limited relation to any specific buyer's actual compute experience.

3. On token price inflation

"The price for a million tokens has doubled since December 1st of last year to about $2.21, which is a mixture of input/output token prices average-weighted by consumption." — Carmen Lee Significance: Specific, dated, consumption-weighted data point directly contradicting the inference-commoditization consensus. Non-consensus in direction and magnitude.

4. On supply-chain friction in announced capacity

"It's not that easy to bring any GPU online. You hear about big data center builds, but they don't translate to immediate GPU availability. You need the servers, colocation, and optical fiber. The stars have to be aligned." — Carmen Lee Significance: Structural supply-constraint argument with identified bottlenecks — supports prices remaining elevated longer than announced-capex models predict. Note: Lee has a commercial interest in tighter supply.

Disagreements & Conviction

TENSION 1: H100 index as a workable hedging instrument given chip heterogeneity The hosts raise fungibility as a structural obstacle. Lee accepts basis risk but argues normalization across 150,000+ daily prices makes it manageable. Conviction: moderate-to-high from Lee — she explicitly names and quantifies the risk rather than dismissing it. However, the 38% same-chip performance variance she published herself is the strongest evidence for the skeptical side. The "daily vol" definitional ambiguity further complicates commercial viability assessment.

TENSION 2: GPU depreciation — Lee's data vs. market narrative Lee's data shows second-year H100 residual at ~85 cents, third-year at ~84 cents — far shallower than consensus depreciation assumptions. Conviction: high but publicly retreated from. Quote: "I have the data, but I'm not going to argue against the market narrative." Two caveats: (1) this is last year's data on a rapidly evolving asset class; (2) Lee operates a refurbished chip business with direct commercial interest in high residual values. Independent verification warranted before building into underwriting models.

TENSION 3: Announced data center builds vs. actual GPU supply availability Lee explicitly pushes back on the equation of capex announcements with near-term supply. Conviction: high and unhedged in her language. The supply-chain dependency logic (servers → colo → fiber → GPUs online) is independently plausible. Commercial interest noted: tighter supply benefits her exchange and index volumes.

TENSION 4: Competing indices diverge — methodology dispute is unresolved Lee declines to claim superiority, deflecting to "the market will vote." This is an absence of conviction, not a resolution. The CME contract will settle to Silicon Data's index; if that index systematically diverges from what participants pay, the futures market fails. An additional layer: Lee is simultaneously CEO of the index provider (Silicon Data) and a competing spot marketplace (Compute Exchange). No firewall, governance structure, or methodology independence is discussed in the transcript. This dual-hat conflict is the cross-cutting risk in every index-integrity discussion.

TENSION 5 (Internal): Bubble deflection vs. implicit constructive framework Lee disclaims forward guidance ("as an index provider, I cannot give forward guidance") then immediately offers a DCF framework suggesting machine-level GPU economics are "pretty straightforward" and currently justifiable. The deflection is formal; the substance is moderately bullish. No actual numbers support the framework in the transcript — it is unverifiable.

TENSION 6: Cerebras/inference-chip heterogeneity — question not answered Joe explicitly asks whether an H100 index is adequate for someone "running inference on some servers or TPUs" given that inference chips like Cerebras differ from training chips. Lee does not engage and pivots to data methodology. The evasion is signal. If inference providers increasingly use non-Nvidia or non-H100 architectures, the H100 index is a structurally imperfect hedge for them, and the basis risk is not just cross-provider but cross-architecture. This is a material gap in the product's inference use-case that was raised and not resolved.

Investment Implications

1. GPU residual values near par challenges fast-depreciation assumptions (if confirmed) First-order: GPU cloud lessors and data center operators may carry assets worth far more than book value if depreciating on standard 3–5 year schedules. ROI on GPU CapEx is higher than consensus models assume. Second-order (inference): Durable collateral values could accelerate debt financing of GPU fleets and drive more aggressive capacity builds than current supply forecasts embed — squeezing the "AI CapEx slowdown" trade. Affected: CoreWeave, GPU cloud lessors, DLR, EQIX, MSFT/GOOGL/META/AMZN CapEx credibility. Time horizon: 12–24 months. Caveat: Lee's data is from last year and she has a commercial interest in the conclusion. Treat as hypothesis requiring independent verification.

2. Token price doubling invalidates near-term inference-commoditization consensus First-order: API providers and inference-layer companies have pricing power now; the "inference to zero" trade is premature. Second-order (inference): AI-native SaaS companies that embedded falling token costs into their unit economics and fixed customer pricing face input cost inflation, not relief. The second-order victim is the "AI integration is nearly free" assumption in SaaS margin models. Affected: Long: NVDA/AMD via demand pull. Watch: AI-native SaaS with high token COGS and fixed-price enterprise contracts. Time horizon: Near-term; watch 2026 earnings call disclosures.

3. B200 and A100 spot price re-inflation signals demand acceleration, not saturation First-order: The spot compute market contradicts the AI spending-peak thesis. Even the most commoditized chip generation (A100, +10–15% in three months) is re-inflating. Second-order (inference): If B200 spot exceeds launch price, contracted supply was insufficient — pointing to Nvidia pricing power on Blackwell and TSMC capacity as the binding constraint, not demand. Affected: NVDA, TSMC, colocation/power names (VST, NRG, CEG), short interest on "AI spending peak" thesis. Time horizon: 6–18 months.

4. CME listing introduces speculative capital that amplifies GPU price cycles First-order: Financial settlement plus 20–30% (definitionally ambiguous) volatility means early open interest will be dominated by directional speculators, not hedgers — standard early commodity market pattern. Second-order (inference): Speculative flows on a thin, financially settled index may amplify spot price expectations without affecting physical supply. AI startups using futures as a hedge face basis risk and speculative distortion simultaneously in the early period. The instrument's most immediate beneficiaries are large enough to absorb basis risk (hyperscalers, large GPU clouds) — not the SMEs most in need of price certainty. Affected: CME Group (fee revenue), DRW/Cumberland (market-making), AI startup working capital management. Time horizon: 0–18 months post-CFTC approval.

5. 38% same-chip performance variance creates unpriced quality premium First-order: Buyers with verified compute can extract an effective 38% cost advantage versus random allocation — a massive edge for training and large-context inference workloads. Second-order (inference): As this variance becomes widely known, it will pressure hyperscalers to offer certified-performance tiers. Bare-metal GPU providers without verification face quality-discount repricing. Compute Exchange and similar verification layers become strategically valuable M&A targets. Affected: AWS/Azure/GCP (disclosure pressure), CoreWeave and bare-metal GPU clouds (quality-signaling opportunity or liability), enterprise AI buyers with SLA obligations. Time horizon: 18–36 months.

importance 5/5 · 95 min · Perplexity CEO: Micron Will Be More Valuable Than Meta & How Export Controls Helped Not Hurt China · ▶ source

Perplexity / Aravind Srinivas — Research Memo

Thesis

The AI value stack is shifting from model capability to orchestration and interface ownership: whoever controls the layer that converts model intelligence into high-value output captures durable margin, while pure-play model providers face commoditization as open-source catches frontier. Power — not capital or chips — is the binding three-year constraint on AI capacity expansion, and the companies that own permitted, powered land extract structural scarcity rent. Perplexity's answer engine was always customer acquisition; the real business is agentic deep research, and revenue has more than tripled in 2026 YTD.

Key Points

  • Answer engine = lead gen, not the product. Pro/Max subscription revenue comes from deep research and agentic workflows, not search answers. Srinivas frames every early-stage AI product as a funnel into the frontier product layer.
  • Google's AI Mode is a functional copy of Perplexity. Srinivas claims credit for changing Google's core interface — same font, inline citations, bolding, suggested follow-ups — and states it is "still not as good." He frames this as validation, not threat, because the frontier has already moved to agents.
  • Google is specifically behind on coding models. Srinivas says Google "underestimated the importance of coding models, so they are behind the frontier right now" — a distinct, falsifiable, near-term call separate from the interface-copy argument.
  • Chat interface is structurally incompatible with advertising. Top Google advertisers (Amazon, Booking.com, Expedia) depend on exploratory, vibes-based user intent — which flows to Meta/Instagram, not an objective answer engine. Explicitly bearish on a $100–200B ad business for OpenAI.
  • Model commoditization is the central structural risk for AI labs. "If you're just a reseller of tokens, you have no business because the model will get commoditized." Open-source models closing on frontier quality within 12 months is presented as the expected case, not a tail risk.
  • Orchestration is the differentiator; token value per watt per user is the key metric. Perplexity's claim: it orchestrates across models (not just tools/files), which Anthropic and OpenAI cannot do. This multi-model routing is the basis for its efficiency argument.
  • Micron could exceed Meta's market cap in 6–12 months. Grounded in bottleneck logic: HBM is the binding constraint; whatever is the bottleneck commands the price. Phrased deliberately cautiously ("might not be inconceivable").
  • Power is the three-year bottleneck, and public resistance compounds it. Permitting, land, turbines, cooling — not capital — are the rate-limiters. Srinivas says resistance will "continue and get worse" based on misinformation about data center water/power consumption.
  • Revenue more than tripled since January 2026. Only hard financial datapoint disclosed. No absolute figures given.
  • Local/hybrid compute is the architecture for durable AI without "going bankrupt." Continuously learning local models reduce context-window costs and address privacy; Perplexity positions itself as the orchestrator across local + server.
  • Team of 400 today; maybe 800–1,000 in two years. Argues AI enables multi-billion-dollar companies built with 40 people — capital efficiency thesis for the sector.
  • OpenAI IPO financial readiness questioned — but only off-camera. Host attributes a pre-show comment to Srinivas that OpenAI isn't financially ready for an IPO. Srinivas deflects on-record without confirming or denying.

Best Quotes

1. On Google's AI Mode as derivative:

"Nobody ever wanted to ship an answer engine at Google. Nobody wanted to tinker with the interface that made them $250 billion a year. And now you look at AI mode, it looks exactly like Perplexity. There's not even any difference—the font, the citations, the specific bolding of inline text, inline hyperlinks, suggested follow-ups. The whole experience is literally looking like Perplexity, except it's still not as good." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Frames Google's AI Mode as defensive imitation, not innovation — and asserts quality inferiority. If accurate, implies sustained execution risk for Alphabet's search transition and an open window at the quality frontier.

2. On chat's structural incompatibility with advertising:

"Who's the number one advertiser on Google? Amazon. Number two is Booking.com. Number three or four is Expedia. How do you book your hotels or flights? Do you book it on ChatGPT or Google? [Host: Google.] Exactly. The interface is less about conversations and more about exploration. When the decision-making is subjective and vibes-based, you don't need an objective answer engine. That's why I'm bearish on advertising taking off in the chat interface." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: A mechanistic argument — not a vibe — against the OpenAI advertising bull case. Travel/e-commerce, the two largest Google ad verticals, don't convert in a chat interface.

3. On orchestration as the true value layer:

"If you're just a reseller of tokens, you have no business because the model will get commoditized. We differentiate ourselves at Perplexity because we don't just orchestrate across tools and files; we also orchestrate across models. That is the differentiation Anthropic and OpenAI cannot claim. We can increase the token value per watt per user. The most important metric in AI is token value per watt per user." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Names the sector's structural fault line and introduces a metric (token value per watt per user) that reframes how AI infrastructure and application companies should be evaluated.

4. On the Micron/Meta relative value call:

"It might not be inconceivable that Micron, the supplier of HBM, might be more valuable than Meta in the next 6 to 12 months." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Deliberately hedged phrasing, but the bottleneck-rent logic is stated with higher conviction. Directionally actionable as a framework for relative positioning between AI infrastructure layers and application-layer platform companies.

Disagreements & Conviction

1. OpenAI's market position — generalized hypothetical, not an explicit bearish call Srinivas opens by arguing that any company, regardless of advantage, "can be put in a position where they're no longer the kings. They're fighting from behind. That's the state of the field." The host takes this as an OpenAI-specific diagnosis; when pressed directly ("Do you perceive them as a dominant leader right now?"), Srinivas says "Yes" — dominant in consumer search. He decouples this from financial IPO readiness but does not confirm the pre-show IPO-readiness comment on record. Conviction: Low/shifting. Investors should not overweight Srinivas's bearishness on OpenAI based on this exchange; the on-record position is more nuanced than the framing suggests. [Note: Host attributes a pre-show comment that Srinivas thinks OpenAI isn't ready for an IPO. Srinivas neither confirms nor contests this in the transcript.]

2. Chat interface cannot sustain a large advertising business — High conviction Explicitly and unqualifiedly bearish: "That's why I'm bearish on advertising taking off in the chat interface." The argument is structural (user intent mismatch, trust corruption) with named advertiser support. Directly challenges a key OpenAI monetization assumption. Conviction: High. This is the clearest non-consensus stake in the conversation.

3. Micron more valuable than Meta in 6–12 months — Provocative framing, moderate underlying logic The specific market cap claim is deliberately hedged and faces a very wide gap to close. The bottleneck-rent logic beneath it is stated with more conviction. Read as: directional argument that HBM suppliers are undervalued relative to application-layer companies, not a literal price target. Conviction: Medium on direction, low on specific timeline and magnitude.

4. "Frontier models are overrated" — Host vs. guest semantic reframe Host argues basic tasks don't need frontier models. Srinivas reframes rather than concedes: "Frontier doesn't mean a frontier model; it means whatever is the frontier outcome you can have right now." Introduces orchestration layer as the actual differentiator. Both positions are actually compatible — this resolves as a semantic distinction, not a genuine disagreement. Conviction on reframe: High. Self-serving for Perplexity's positioning.

5. Internal tension: Answer engine as "lead gen" vs. claiming credit for changing Google Srinivas says the answer engine "was always a lead gen" for frontier products, while simultaneously arguing it "changed Google.com more than any product manager at Google has ever done." Both positions held with high conviction. If search was just acquisition scaffolding, then Google copying the interface is strategically irrelevant; if it was the defining product achievement, it wasn't just scaffolding. The brand equity vs. monetization decoupling creates a latent risk if search traffic fails to convert to agentic revenue.

6. Internal tension: Models commoditize vs. models as frontier-staying mechanism "If you're just a reseller of tokens, you have no business." But also: "Building models is a way to stay at the frontier." Not reconciled. The implication — model builders must also own interfaces to survive — is not explicitly drawn, leaving the terminal fate of API-first labs (Anthropic) structurally unresolved.

Investment Implications

I. HBM is the extractable rent in the AI stack Srinivas's bottleneck logic: whatever constrains throughput commands pricing power. HBM memory bandwidth is the binding physical constraint on training and inference at scale. First-order: MU, SK Hynix price to the bottleneck, not to cost. Second-order: the consensus bottleneck trade is NVDA; if pricing power migrates one layer down to memory, NVDA faces relative compression while HBM suppliers benefit from hyperscaler capex that funds their revenue. Meta's own capex expansion is a direct Micron revenue tailwind — Meta's scale is Micron's customer, not its competitor. Affected: MU (long), SK Hynix (long), NVDA (relative), META (capex → supplier revenue) Time horizon: 12–24 months [External reference: Srinivas does not cite specific market cap figures for MU or META; relative-value gap is large by any current market estimate and 6–12 month timeline is aggressive.]

II. Model commoditization undermines pure-play AI lab valuations Open-source reaching frontier quality within 12 months is Srinivas's expected case, not a tail risk. Enterprises fine-tuning open models ("Absolutely. It's in their incentive to bring down the cost.") accelerates the dynamic. If orchestration/interface captures margin, the terminal value of API-first model providers shrinks. Venture capital flowing into model companies subsidizes cheap tokens, which accelerates its own commoditization. Beneficiaries: enterprises with proprietary data and distribution that can fine-tune open models at near-zero marginal cost (META's Llama ecosystem), and model-agnostic platforms. Affected: Anthropic, OpenAI (private — valuation risk); META (Llama strategic moat), enterprise SaaS with proprietary data (CRM, NOW, WDAY), hyperscalers offering managed fine-tuning (MSFT Azure, AMZN Bedrock) Time horizon: 18–36 months for full repricing; leading indicators in 12 months

III. Google's AI Mode cannibalizes high-CPM queries without replacing ad revenue AI Mode resolves high-intent transactional queries (travel, e-commerce) without delivering users to advertisers. CPM for navigational/transactional queries deflates as AI answers reduce click-through. Google is simultaneously cannibalizing its highest-value ad inventory and unable to monetize the replacement interface as effectively. Second-order: Amazon, Booking, Expedia diversify ad spend toward social (META, SNAP) and direct channels. Inference: Google's 2025–2026 revenue resilience may mask query-mix deterioration — high-CPM commercial queries converting to zero-click AI answers. Affected: GOOGL (structural pressure on Search revenue quality), META (ad budget beneficiary), BKNG, EXPE, AMZN (advertiser budget reallocation) Time horizon: Already underway; material P&L impact within 2–3 years

IV. Google's coding-model gap creates an opening in developer wallet share Srinivas explicitly: Google "underestimated the importance of coding models, so they are behind the frontier right now." This is separate from the AI Mode interface argument and directly relevant to the developer tooling market. Google has structural advantages (TPU fleet, data, Search distribution) but a late-mover disadvantage in the coding tier that could prove durable given developer platform stickiness. The MSFT/GitHub Copilot/Cursor ecosystem benefits from this gap continuing. Affected: GOOGL (coding moat lag), MSFT (GitHub Copilot/Azure beneficiary), Cursor (private), Perplexity (private) Time horizon: 12–24 months before coding-model gap closes or widens decisively

V. Power is a structural multi-year bottleneck with compounding social headwinds Power — not capital, not chips, not talent — is the binding constraint for at least three years. Social/political resistance to data center buildout is Srinivas's forward call (resistance "will continue and get worse"), and it is structurally underpriced in investment debate (which focuses on AI demand, not supply buildability). Scarcity rent accrues to incumbents with already-permitted, already-powered facilities. Nuclear becomes differentiated for co-location due to 24/7 baseload and lower permitting friction narrative. Affected: NEE, CEG, VST (power generation), EQIX, IRM, DLR (incumbent data center REITs with existing permits), CCJ/UUUU (uranium), CoreWeave/Nebius (private, if land/power owned); short — new merchant data center entrants without land/power position Time horizon: 2–5 years; near-term catalysts in utility rate cases and permitting decisions

VI. Local/edge compute is the underpriced infrastructure call Srinivas argues the winning architecture is a hybrid local/server orchestration layer — privacy-driven, latency-driven, cost-driven. If local models become "good enough" for a material fraction of inference as open-source closes on frontier, cloud inference's share of total AI compute shrinks. Hyperscaler capex projections baked into current valuations may overstate durable cloud inference revenue. AAPL's on-device inference investment is more strategically significant than the "Apple is behind on AI" consensus narrative. Affected: AAPL (on-device inference moat, underappreciated), QCOM (NPU in Snapdragon), AMD (Ryzen AI client), cloud hyperscalers (long-term inference share at risk) Time horizon: 2–4 years for material volume shift; 12-month setup trade in device-layer beneficiaries

Abivax (ABVX) & Nectar Therapeutics — Research Memo

Recorded June 8, 2026 | Guest: Adam May, specialist biotech long/short investor

Thesis

Abivax's Phase 3 UC maintenance trial delivered best-in-class efficacy — matching Rinvoq on clinical remission delta and roughly doubling it on the GI-preferred endoscopic remission endpoint — without Rinvoq's black-box safety profile. The post-data collapse from ~$185 to ~$100 was driven by a cancer signal May argues is demonstrably noise: after reclassifying one non-cancer case and four non-melanoma skin cancers, only two common solid-tumor cancers remain with no mechanistic pathway. At ~$100, May believes the market is fully pricing in a black-box warning it may not receive, creating asymmetric skew he frames as 100% near-term upside and perhaps 200% over twelve months.

Key Points

Efficacy — the setup entering maintenance data - The prior induction trial ranked Abivax as the third most efficacious drug ever studied in ulcerative colitis — a high bar entering the maintenance readout. - May's own pre-release estimate was a 25% placebo-adjusted clinical remission delta; the actual result came in at 40% (50mg) and 39% (25mg) — a material upside surprise on his own conservative baseline. - The independent Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) had reviewed 80–90% of trial data before the readout with no new safety signals — making the post-release cancer surprise more anomalous, not less, and strengthening the statistical-noise argument.

Efficacy vs. best-in-class comparator - Clinical remission delta matched/exceeded Rinvoq (JAK inhibitor), previously considered the ceiling for UC efficacy. - Endoscopic remission delta: Abivax 38% vs. Rinvoq 18% — approximately 2× on the endpoint GI physicians weight most because it is objective (scope-verified, not patient-reported). - Rinvoq carries a black-box warning for cancer, severe/fatal infections, blood clots, and cardiovascular events; Abivax does not currently carry one.

The cancer signal — May's case-by-case decomposition - Raw headline: 7 cancer cases (high-dose arm) vs. 1 (placebo) — this is what drove the selloff. - Reclassification: 1 case was colonic dysplasia (precancerous condition, not cancer); 4 cases were non-melanoma skin cancer (15–20× more prevalent than other cancers, typically resolved in a 15-minute outpatient procedure). - Residual: 2 "real" cancers in the 50mg arm; 0 in the 25mg arm; 0 in placebo — common solid tumors (prostate, breast), no anatomical clustering. - Mechanistic argument: drug is neither genotoxic nor immunosuppressive; severe infections were actually more common in the placebo arm, which is the opposite of what immunosuppression would produce. - DSMB context (above) reinforces: an independent safety board saw nothing alarming through ~85% of the trial. - Management error: the inflated cancer count is partly self-inflicted — the presentation included non-cancer events in the cancer tally, triggering a selloff the underlying data does not support.

Valuation / scenario framing - At ~$100 (as of June 8): May says this already fully prices in a black-box warning. - Blue-sky scenario (no black box + Crohn's disease approval): $8–10B peak sales potential. May describes the skew as "huge" but does not assign an explicit probability to the regulatory outcome. - Near-term downside limited by UC efficacy: the drug unambiguously works for ulcerative colitis — that is not in dispute and sets a floor. - Key residual bear risk May acknowledges: Part 2 data could add cancer cases; market is partly waiting on that.

Why the mispricing persists - Analytical barrier: reconstructing the case-level cancer count requires work most market participants haven't done. - Sell-side downgrade cascade: mechanical, coverage-driven — not necessarily based on case-level reclassification. - Part 2 fear: investors may be holding off pending the next data drop.

Nectar Therapeutics (no ticker confirmed in transcript) - Stock pulled back from ~$100 to mid-$50s with no fundamental change to the alopecia areata signal. - May attributes weakness to: (1) ongoing jury trial litigation vs. Eli Lilly — outside typical biotech investor frameworks, creating holder mismatch; (2) competitive overhang from Q32 Bio hyping their own alopecia areata program. - May says "I'm at a loss as to why the sell-off has been so severe" — admits incomplete explanatory model. - Ranked explicitly as the less mispriced of the two positions; Abivax is the priority call.

Best Quotes

1. The efficacy headline

"Abivax's maintenance data came in with a 'four handle'—40% at the high dose and 39% at the low dose. It matched and exceeded Rinvoq on clinical remission delta. Even more impressively, on endoscopic remission, which is a more objective endpoint that GI doctors favor, Abivax crushed Rinvoq, with a 38% delta compared to Rinvoq's 18%." — Adam May

Significance: The 2× endoscopic remission advantage is the buried lead. This is the endpoint prescribers trust most, and it is directly relevant to real-world adoption independent of label language.

2. Dismantling the cancer signal

"You are left with two 'real' cancers in the 50mg arm, zero in the 25mg arm, and zero in placebo. These two were common cancers—prostate and breast—with no clustering. There is no 'smoking gun' mechanism for how this drug would cause cancer; it is not genotoxic, and it is not immunosuppressive, as severe infections were more common in the placebo arm. This is statistical noise." — Adam May

Significance: The mechanistic argument is more durable than a statistical one — it is testable at FDA and in the literature, and it directly attacks the bear thesis at its foundation.

3. Why the market is wrong without being irrational

"I don't believe in efficient markets. I'm amazed at the things the market is able to ignore. It takes a lot of work to calculate these numbers, and I think people either haven't done it or are worried that more cases will come out in the part two data." — Adam May

Significance: Identifies the mispricing mechanism as analytical friction, not information asymmetry — and honestly flags the one live bear risk (Part 2 data) he is not dismissing.

4. The valuation anchor

"I think at $100, you are pricing in a black box warning. The blue sky case is a hit in Crohn's disease and no black box, which could make it an 8-10 billion dollar peak sales drug. The skew is huge." — Adam May

Significance: Explicit scenario framing with a peak sales handle. Falsifiable: if current price does not fully discount a black box, the downside is larger than May assumes.

Disagreements & Conviction

Tension May's Position Counter-Position May's Conviction Status
Cancer signal: noise vs. real Demonstrably false after case reclassification; no mechanism Market at ~$100 and sell-side downgrades assign non-trivial probability to real risk Very high — uses "demonstrably false"; provides specific case decomposition Unresolved; Part 2 data is the arbiter
Market efficiency in biotech Explicitly rejects; attributes non-recovery to analytical burden Host: stock has had a week to recover and hasn't — soft EMH argument Firm — "I don't believe in efficient markets" Structural disagreement; no resolution in episode

Management competence One-time presentation error Mishandling the most sensitive safety disclosure is a durable execution risk May does not address N/A — May does not engage this tension Gap in thesis — inference that he is discounting operational risk
Nectar: signal intact vs. priced for deterioration Alopecia signal legitimate; selloff is holder mismatch and competitive noise Market pricing reflects litigation tail and potential competitive displacement Lower — "I'm at a loss" Less resolved than the Abivax call; explicitly ranked secondary

Investment Implications

1. Endoscopic remission gap is underweighted in consensus bear case The market debate has collapsed to "black box vs. no black box," bypassing prescriber behavior. If GI physicians prioritize the objective endpoint (endoscopic remission, where Abivax leads 38% vs. 18%), real-world adoption could be strong even under a black box — the same way Rinvoq is prescribed despite its warnings. Peak sales estimates that hard-discount a black box may be systematically too low. Assets: ABVX; AbbVie (ABBV) on Rinvoq UC franchise share. Horizon: 12–24 months (approval → early commercial scripts). Confidence: Efficacy differential — TRANSCRIPT-SUPPORTED; prescriber behavior under black box — MODEL INFERENCE.

2. Sell-side downgrade cascade is mechanical, not fundamental Institutional holders with consensus-dependency requirements are structural sellers regardless of the case-level analysis. Recovery requires a specific catalyst forcing sell-side re-engagement: Part 2 data, FDA advisory committee, or label negotiation disclosure. Without a timing view on that catalyst, the asymmetric thesis carries a carry/patience risk separate from the binary outcome risk. Assets: ABVX; any small/mid biotech dragged down in the June 1 sector selloff. Horizon: Near-term to 6 months, catalyst-dependent. Confidence: TRANSCRIPT-SUPPORTED (downgrade cascade); duration of dislocation — MODEL INFERENCE.

3. Lower-dose arm (25mg) may carry a cleaner safety profile than headline suggests Zero cancers in the 25mg arm vs. two in the 50mg arm. Even under a worst-case black box outcome for the 50mg UC indication, a 25mg Crohn's program could theoretically present a cleaner dose-specific safety profile. The market's binary black-box framing ignores this pathway. Note: May does not explicitly make this argument — this is inference. Assets: ABVX; potential major pharma acquirer with existing Crohn's franchise. Horizon: 18–36 months (Crohn's trial readout). Confidence: MODEL INFERENCE — dose-specific differential is in the transcript; the Crohn's pathway argument is extrapolation.

4. Nectar — holder mismatch, not signal deterioration Biotech specialists (the natural buyer base) are self-selected out due to jury trial literacy. Two discrete, independently removable overhangs (Lilly litigation outcome; Q32 Bio data read) are compressing a stock whose drug signal is described as intact. Re-rating path is event sequencing, not new clinical data. Assets: Nectar Therapeutics (ticker NOT confirmed in transcript — verify before acting); Q32 Bio (QTTB) as a binary read-across on the alopecia competitive narrative. Horizon: 6–18 months; litigation timeline unknown. Confidence: Holder mismatch thesis — GUEST-SUPPORTED; Q32 binary catalyst — MODEL INFERENCE. Competitive landscape drug/company specifics (beyond Q32 Bio) are outside-knowledge not drawn from transcript.

5. Crohn's optionality is unpriced in the bear scenario At $100 with a black box priced in, the Crohn's indication appears to be valued at near-zero. Crohn's is a larger addressable market with significant unmet need and is the primary driver of the $8–10B peak sales figure. Even partial probability on Crohn's success represents unrecognized option value. Assets: ABVX. Horizon: 18–36 months.
